Given that most organs can not be removed from your body without permanent or fatal damage to you, the only viable position for it would be post-mortem removal (aka, what we currently know as voluntary unpaid organ donations). Creating financial incentives for the post-mortem removal likely would result in more "donators" (though this would not be the right word anymore), but also causes issues such as

  1. who ends up getting the organs - donators would seek to get the most out of their organ sale, but then you'd end up with a system where only rich people would get replacement organs, rather than those who actually need them (i.e. an old, morbidly obese and chain-smoking businessman who'd get ten more years out of the transplant, as opposed to a poor but young, healthy person who might get several decades).
  2. making personal care for the body less appealing - why not drink your liver to death and smoke till you lung collapses? There's always replacements to be had, so long as you have the money (though this is a general scarcity problem that comes with higher supply in general).
  3. A (potential) surge in murders for organ harvesting. However, this effect also could be averted by the higher supply and hence lower prices for individual organs.

Rest assured, I don't think that the current system is ideal, but I think the incentive for organ donation should be a moral one rather than a financial one. Turning the human body into a piece of meat with choice cuts to be had is rather unnerving to me.
